steps.premise: Copies may still be on a rack when volunteers come to restock it.
steps.action: Count the remaining copies at each site before putting out new ones.
steps.consequence: Volunteers can adjust next week's bundle there to match demand.
steps.quote: Count the copies left at each pickup spot before replacing them. Next week's bundles can then be sized to the number of people actually taking a paper there.

steps.premise: Rain can soak a stack outside a shop.
steps.action: Put the papers in a covered dispenser.
steps.consequence: The copies stay readable until pickup.
steps.quote: A stack by an outside shop door can soak through in one shower. A covered dispenser keeps the papers readable until someone comes for them.

steps.premise: Several buildings on the delivery route have similar names.
steps.action: Label each bundle with its street number.
steps.consequence: The carrier can take it to the right lobby.
steps.quote: Some buildings on the route have nearly identical names. Print the street number on each bundle so the delivery volunteer can find the correct lobby.

steps.premise: Some residents seldom visit the shops.
steps.action: Add a box to the signup slip for residents to request home delivery.
steps.consequence: Residents who seldom visit a pickup site can still receive a copy.
steps.quote: Ask residents to mark a small box on the signup slip if they prefer a doorstep copy. People who rarely get to the shops would still receive the bulletin.

steps.premise: Outdated event listings can linger on crowded shop counters.
steps.action: Display the edition date prominently on the front.
steps.consequence: Readers can identify the current week's issue.
steps.quote: Lists of events go stale quickly on a crowded counter. Give the issue date a prominent place on the front so readers can pick out this week's edition.

steps.premise: A substitute carrier could miss a shop hidden in an alley.
steps.action: Include a picture of the shop entrance on the route sheet.
steps.consequence: The carrier can recognize the delivery point.
steps.quote: A volunteer covering an unfamiliar route may miss a shop tucked down an alley. A photograph of its entrance on the route sheet makes the handoff easier to find.

steps.premise: If a carrier arrives before a shop opens, the bundle must be brought back.
steps.action: Agree on a delivery time with each shopkeeper.
steps.consequence: The carrier can hand over the papers without making a second circuit.
steps.quote: Arrange a delivery time with each shopkeeper. A bundle arriving before the doors open otherwise has to travel around the route a second time.

steps.premise: A crate holding hundreds of papers is unwieldy on stairs.
steps.action: Divide it into smaller bundles before sending it out from the print shop.
steps.consequence: Volunteers can carry the copies in manageable loads.
steps.quote: Stairs make a crate of several hundred copies awkward to handle. Split it into smaller bundles at the print shop so volunteers can carry one manageable load at a time.

steps.premise: A subscriber moves to another address within the neighborhood.
steps.action: Provide a phone number where readers can report a move.
steps.consequence: Delivery can continue at the new address and papers stop piling up at the old one.
steps.quote: Give readers a phone number for address changes. Someone who moves within the neighborhood can keep receiving a copy, and the old doorstep stops accumulating papers.

steps.premise: The regular carrier might fall ill on delivery morning.
steps.action: Assign each route a backup carrier familiar with its stops.
steps.consequence: That week's bulletin can still reach its readers.
steps.quote: Paper carriers sometimes fall ill on delivery morning. Pair each route with a backup who already knows the stops so that week's issue still goes out.

steps.premise: Some readers have trouble reading the regular print.
steps.action: Print copies in larger type.
steps.consequence: The bulletin is easier for those readers to read.
steps.quote: A copy printed in larger type would help readers who struggle with the regular edition.

steps.premise: The printer needs a quantity for large-type copies.
steps.action: Have the library collect requests for that edition.
steps.consequence: The printer can prepare the requested number.
steps.quote: A copy printed in larger type would help readers who struggle with the regular edition. Let the library take requests so the printer knows how many to prepare.

steps.premise: Some readers shop only once each week.
steps.action: Restock the bulletin racks on a regular day.
steps.consequence: Readers can plan their trip to pick up a fresh issue.
steps.quote: Pick a consistent day for replenishing the racks. Readers who make just one shopping trip a week can then plan to collect a fresh copy.

steps.premise: A delivered copy can be destroyed after it arrives.
steps.action: Keep a few spare copies at the packing table for replacement requests.
steps.consequence: A reader can still obtain that week's issue.
steps.quote: Set aside a few copies at the packing table for replacement requests. A reader whose dog shreds the morning delivery can still get that issue.

steps.premise: A lobby cleanup can remove papers left outside the permitted location.
steps.action: Ask the apartment caretaker where papers may be left and use the approved shelf.
steps.consequence: Copies stay available after the morning cleanup.
steps.quote: Ask an apartment caretaker where residents are allowed to leave printed material. A stack on the approved shelf will survive the morning lobby cleanup.

steps.premise: Sale leaflets can draw attention away from the bulletin rack at checkout.
steps.action: Place a small sign above the rack saying the paper is free.
steps.consequence: Shoppers have a reason to pick up a bulletin.
steps.quote: A full rack by the checkout is easy to overlook among the sale leaflets. A small sign above it telling shoppers the bulletin is free gives them a reason to take one.

steps.premise: Two carriers can take the same route if the sheet remains unsigned.
steps.action: Have carriers initial the route sheet when collecting a route.
steps.consequence: The following carrier can identify and choose an unclaimed route.
steps.quote: One unsigned route sheet can leave two people delivering the same bundle. Have carriers initial the sheet when they collect a route so the next person picks an open one.

steps.premise: A planned holiday street closure can block part of a delivery route.
steps.action: Mark announced closures on the map for that week.
steps.consequence: The carrier can approach the block from the opposite end.
steps.quote: A holiday street closure can cut a carrier off halfway around the block. Note announced closures on the week's route map so the carrier can enter from the other end.

steps.premise: A reader's neighbor may want to know where papers are available.
steps.action: Print a list of pickup points inside each issue.
steps.consequence: The reader can tear out the list and give it to the neighbor.
steps.quote: Display a pickup list inside the bulletin. Readers can tear it out for a neighbor who keeps asking where to find a copy.

steps.premise: Clinic staff can start work before shops open.
steps.action: Leave a bulletin in the clinic staff break room.
steps.consequence: Workers can read the issue during their shift.
steps.quote: Put a copy in the staff break room at the neighborhood clinic. Workers who come in before the shops open would have a chance to read it on their shift.

steps.premise: A household plans to be away for a given week.
steps.action: Let the household suspend doorstep delivery for that week.
steps.consequence: Old papers will not accumulate while the residents are away.
steps.quote: Let households pause a doorstep delivery for a specified week. They can go away without coming back to a pile of old bulletins.
